raw-columns.t: A slice of the customer table: **seven columns** for six customers. Most describe the customer, one is a date, and the last, **churned**, is the outcome. The first question is which columns a model may legitimately use.

candidate-features.t: The green columns are the **candidate features**: tenure, usage, tickets, price and days idle. They describe each customer **before** the decision, so they are the information the model is allowed to look at.

target-column.t: The blue column is the **target** (churned_30d), the outcome we want to predict. Features go in, the target is what should come out. Keeping the two separate is the basic structure of supervised learning.

valid-feature.t: **Days idle** counts how long ago the customer was last active, so it is known on the prediction day. Because it exists **before** the outcome, it is a valid feature, and a useful one.

another-feature.t: **Support tickets** are also counted before the 30-day window starts, so they are valid too. Every feature passes the same test: **would we know this value on the day we predict?**

leaky-feature.t: The **closed date** is filled in for every churner and empty for every customer who stayed, so it predicts the target **6 out of 6**. That perfection is the warning sign: the column contains the answer.

prediction-time-check.t: Ask the test on day 0: the customer has **not cancelled yet**, so there is **no closed date** to read. A column that only exists after the outcome cannot be a feature, however well it predicts.

remove-leakage.t: The closed-date column fades out because it is removed **before any training or testing**. A model built with it would look perfect in testing and then fail in real use, where the date does not exist yet.

final-feature-set.t: **X** is the five valid features and **y** is churned_30d. **Remember:** a feature is valid only if it is known at prediction time. A strong predictor that breaks this rule is **leakage**, not skill.
